Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National | Technology GSSTI Director urges passage of national space law to unlock Ghana’s share of US$680bn space economy Source : Emmanuel Tetteh 16 November 2026 8:13pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Director of the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI), Dr Joseph Tandoh, has called for the urgent establishment of the Ghana Space Agency and the passage of a national space law to regulate the country's space activities, protect national interests and unlock economic opportunities in the global space industry.
He said although Ghana had made progress in developing its space policy and securing Cabinet approval for the proposed agency, the absence of an operational regulatory framework was delaying the country's ability to fully participate in the rapidly expanding space economy.
Speaking on the sidelines of the 2026 Ghana Space Conference in Accra on Monday, November 16, Dr Tandoh said Ghana needed to move from policy development to implementation to position itself to benefit from the opportunities in space science and technology.
He recalled Ghana's achievement in 2017 when All Nations University launched GhanaSat, which generated national excitement and demonstrated the country's capacity to participate in space-related activities.
He said Ghana also began developing its national space policy that year, which was subsequently approved by Cabinet in 2022 and unveiled in 2024.
Cabinet further approved the establishment of the Ghana Space Agency in 2025, but Dr Tandoh stressed that the approval did not mean the institution had formally been established.
He said the 2026 conference, running from November 16 to 18, was therefore intended to build understanding of why Ghana needed the agency, its responsibilities and the legal framework required to make it operational.
Dr Tandoh identified three major reasons for establishing the agency: protecting the country, generating economic benefits and building national capacity in space science and technology.
On national protection, he warned that Ghana currently lacked the necessary legal framework to address liabilities and regulate space activities, including incidents involving falling rocket debris or damage caused by space objects.
He noted that although Ghana had signed international instruments such as the Outer Space Treaty, the Rescue Agreement and the Liability Convention, the country had yet to ratify them.
He said the situation raised questions about which institution would be responsible for handling space-related incidents and ensuring that Ghana's interests were protected.
Dr Tandoh also expressed concern about the absence of a regulatory authority to supervise space activities undertaken by universities, private companies and start-ups.
He explained that under the Outer Space Treaty, countries are responsible for authorising and supervising space activities conducted within their territories, whether by government institutions or private entities.
He said the proposed Ghana Space Agency would provide the institutional framework to discharge these responsibilities, making the development and passage of a national space bill particularly urgent.
On the economic opportunities, Dr Tandoh said the global space economy was valued at approximately US$680 billion and grew by 12 per cent in the previous year, generating an estimated US$2 billion daily.
He questioned how Ghana intended to position itself to capture a share of the growing industry, particularly given its geographical location along the Equator.
According to him, Ghana's location offers a strategic advantage for launching rockets into space at potentially lower costs, making the country an attractive destination for companies exploring spaceport development.
He disclosed that several companies had expressed interest in exploring opportunities to establish spaceports in Ghana but stressed that the absence of clear laws and regulations remained a major obstacle to attracting such investments.
Dr Tandoh said enacting the necessary legislation would provide the certainty investors needed to commit resources to the country's space industry.
He also called on Members of Parliament and relevant government ministries to support the proposed space bill when it is presented to Parliament, describing it as essential to Ghana's development.
On capacity building, he said satellite technology had important applications in mining, natural resource management and national security, making it necessary for Ghana to develop its own expertise and technical capabilities.
He argued that the country could not continue relying heavily on foreign partners for satellite imagery and other space-based information, particularly when it needed data to address its own development challenges.
"Nobody understands our problems better than we do, and we cannot always depend on foreign partners for satellite images," he said.
Dr Tandoh said establishing the Ghana Space Agency, backed by appropriate legislation, would help coordinate the country's space activities, attract investment and equip the next generation of Ghanaian professionals with the skills needed to compete in the industry.
He said Ghana must act decisively to ensure it was not left behind as the global space economy expanded.
"Our message is simple: Let us establish the Ghana Space Agency, back it up with the necessary regulations to make it work, and empower the agency to build the capacity of the next generation of space science and technology professionals we need," he added.
